claims.notes: THE BRIDGE ORDINANCE, IN THE FIRST OF THE THREE ISSUES THAT CARRY IT. It is read in full from 1834-05-21 (claim c016 there), which keeps 'faster than on a walk' whole and both signatures; this reading is kept because it is INDEPENDENT — a different issue, a different segmenter column — and because it is the earliest printing in the month, which is what dates the ordinance's publication rather than its passage. Note that neither this reading nor the fuller one gives the ordinance's date of passage: only its number, 16, which places it in the same series as the fifteen clauses of 4 December 1833 read in 1834-01-07 and therefore AFTER the wharfing clause 15. The clerk's surname reads 'Hanwox' here, 'Hanson' in 1834-05-21 and 'Hammon' in 1834-05-28; Harmon is the reading the three support together.

claims.notes: 'TO BE DELIVERED FROM THE WHARF' — the phrase whole, in the only reading of the month that keeps it. The same advertisement is cut in 1834-05-21 (page 3 column 3, lines 2772-2778) and in 1834-05-28 (claim c010 there, where it reads 'juron, to i' / 'rn the flare i sold low if'), so this line is what licenses the supply in the others. WHY IT MATTERS: a hundred barrels of salt landed from the schooner Huron are being sold OFF THE WHARF, cheaper than out of a store, five weeks into the 1834 navigation season. That is a wharf in working use, with goods standing on it, and it is John H. Kinzie's — whose warehouse the same run places opposite Fort Dearborn (1834-05-28, claim c016). THE WHARF IS NOT LOCATED and no reading of this card gives it a street, a bank or a neighbour.

claims.notes: 'MY HOUSE, ON THE WESTERN BANK OF' — the officer speaks in the first person and gives his own dwelling as the county's polling place. The signature is cut away here and is read from 1834-05-28 (claim c009 there), where it survives as 'S. FORB' — Stephen Forbes, who is also the executor named in David Laughton's will in 1834-05-07 (page 3 column 3, lines 2903-2911). The river's name is likewise cut here and whole in the later reading, 'the western bank of Des P[laines]'. WHAT THIS CLAIM ADDS ON ITS OWN is the first-person 'MY house', which the 1834-05-28 reading also carries but which is worth recording twice: a private house on the west bank of the Des Plaines was where every militia-eligible man in Cook county was summoned on the first Saturday in June 1834.

claims.notes: THE SCHOONER HURON, ON THE DAY SHE LANDED KINZIE'S SALT. The marine list of this issue names the Huron on 8 May, and John H. Kinzie's advertisement four columns away offers a hundred barrels of salt 'received per the Huron, to be delivered from the wharf' over a dateline of 12 May (claim c003). Two independent notices in one issue, agreeing on a vessel and a cargo — which is what turns a shipping line into evidence about the wharf. The rest of the list is badly cut and three entries sit inside the transcription's own uncertainty brackets, which are kept.

claims.notes: AN OFFICE PLACED AGAINST A PUBLIC OFFICE — 'adjoining that of the Clerk of the Circuit Court'. That is the only line in the month that sites any part of Cook county's court apparatus, and it does it sideways, in a lawyer's card. It says the Circuit Court Clerk kept a fixed office in the town in May 1834 and that a private office stood next to it; it does NOT say where either was, and no reading in this run supplies a street. The same card is cut differently in 1834-05-07 (page 3 column 1, lines 2630-2633, claim c012 there), which keeps 'ATTORNEY 4 COUNSELLOI' and 'arcuit Cou' — the two readings together are what license 'Circuit Court' here.

claims.notes: THE THIRD INDEPENDENT READING OF THE SAME ADDRESS IN ONE MONTH. Matthias Mason's card runs unchanged from the paper's first issue through May 1834, and 'opposite Graves' Tave[rn]' survives in this issue, in 1834-05-21 (claim c005 there) and in 1834-05-28 (claim c022 there). The dateline 'Nov: 2%, 1' is read as 26 November 1833, the paper's first issue, which is where the card was first read (1833-11-26, claim c020). Recording it in every issue that carries it is what widens the business's evidence window honestly rather than by assertion.

claims.notes: C. & I. HARMON, STILL TRADING IN MAY 1834 — the firm the scan-verified record of the paper's first issue insisted on against a rival transcription's 'C. & L. Harmon'. The initials read 'C. & 1.' twice on this column, which is the same 1-for-I recognition shape the source record warns about, and they are read as C. & I. on the strength of that record (ruling 2 run backwards: where a scan has been read, it outranks the transcription). NO ADDRESS in either notice. The column interleaves two advertisements line by line and John H. Kinzie's dateline of 1 March 1834 belongs to the second of them, not to the Harmon goods, which are dated 5 May 1834; the reading says so rather than letting one dateline stand for both.
